lead: Arkansas homes face spring tornadoes, river flooding and the occasional ice storm. DryFlare helps owners across the state get water out and get drying started fast.
risk: severe storms and tornadoes, river flooding and winter ice storms
why: Arkansas sits where tornado alley meets the lower Mississippi valley. Severe storms roll through every spring, and FEMA has declared more than two dozen major disasters for them since 2000. The Arkansas River flood of 2019 set records from Fort Smith to Little Rock and pushed water into homes and businesses along the river.

Winter brings its own trouble. Ice storms like the one in January 2009 knock out power for days, and pipes freeze in homes built for mild weather. In the Ozarks around Fayetteville and Rogers, hillsides send runoff into basements. In the Delta, flat land and heavy clay soil hold water for a long time. Like Missouri and Oklahoma, Arkansas sees hail damage that leads to roof leaks.
image_alt: Yard and house surrounded by standing water after heavy rain
image_caption: River and flash flooding in Arkansas often leaves water standing around homes for days.
problems: Homes along the Arkansas and White rivers
tips: Insulate pipes in crawl spaces before winter; ice storms often bring multi-day outages.
Check your sump pump each spring if you have a basement.
After hail, have the roof looked at even if you see no leaks yet.
Know your flood zone; FEMA flood maps cover most river towns.
insurance: After severe storms, Arkansas insurers often see a rush of hail claims, so report damage quickly and keep receipts for tarps and emergency repairs.

faq.q: How fast does mold grow after a flood in Arkansas?
faq.a: Mold can start growing within 24 to 48 hours in warm, humid weather like an Arkansas summer. Getting water out and running dehumidifiers right away is the best way to stop it.
